lede: Some crystals hold water inside their structure. This lesson shows how to count it, from a formula and from the masses before and after heating, and how to find any compound's empirical formula from its masses.
can: Define water of crystallisation, hydrated and anhydrous, and work out the Mr of a hydrate.
Heat a hydrated salt to constant mass and use the masses to find x.
Work out empirical and molecular formulae from masses or percentages.

md: Blue copper(II) sulfate crystals crumble to a white powder when they are heated: water locked inside each crystal is driven off. Weigh the solid before and after, and the masses tell you how much water every unit of the crystal held.

md: Some salts crystallise with water **chemically bonded into the crystal structure**: that water is the **water of crystallisation**. A salt that holds it is **hydrated**; with all of it driven off, the salt is **anhydrous**. In a formula, the number after the dot counts the waters in each unit.

stem: Which of these is hydrated: blue $\ce{CuSO4.5H2O}$ crystals, copper(II) sulfate dissolved in water, or the white powder left after heating?

steps.working: Blue $\ce{CuSO4.5H2O}$ crystals: hydrated. The $\ce{.5H2O}$ shows 5 waters bonded into the crystal for every $\ce{CuSO4}$.
steps.decision: Read the number after the dot: it counts the waters that each unit of the crystal holds.

steps.working: Copper(II) sulfate solution: not hydrated, although it is mostly water.
steps.decision: That water surrounds the dissolved salt; it is not bonded into a crystal structure, which is the condition the definition needs.

steps.working: The white powder: anhydrous $\ce{CuSO4}$, with all its water driven off.
steps.decision: Heating removed the water of crystallisation, so nothing follows the dot any more.

prompt: What is meant by the term hydrated?
options: contains water of crystallisation
dissolved in water
has had its water removed
explain: Hydrated describes a solid that still holds water bonded into its crystal structure, as the blue crystals in step 1 of See it do. A solution's water is not bonded into a crystal, and a salt with its water removed is anhydrous.

optionNotes.why: A dissolved salt is surrounded by water, but that water is not bonded into a crystal structure, so the salt is not hydrated.
That describes the anhydrous salt, the white powder; hydrated is the form that still has its water.

twin.prompt: What is meant by the term anhydrous?
options: with all its water of crystallisation removed
dissolved in water
containing water of crystallisation
twin.answer: with all its water of crystallisation removed
twin.explain: Anhydrous means without water of crystallisation: the white powder left once heating has driven all the water out of the crystals.

optionNotes.why: A solution is a salt in water; anhydrous describes a solid with no water bonded into it.
That is what hydrated means; anhydrous is the form after that water has gone.

prompt: How many water molecules are bonded into the crystal for each MgSO₄ unit in MgSO₄·7H₂O?
explain: Read the number after the dot, as step 1 of See it read 5 for copper(II) sulfate: 7H₂O means 7 molecules of water of crystallisation for every MgSO₄.

twin.prompt: How many water molecules are bonded into the crystal for each Ca(NO₃)₂ unit in Ca(NO₃)₂·4H₂O?
twin.explain: The number after the dot counts the waters in each unit: 4H₂O means 4.

alt: A bar for the relative formula mass of Ca(NO3)2.4H2O, 236, split into Ca(NO3)2, 164, and four waters of 18 each, 72.
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 150" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="hy3canMr"><title id="hy3canMr">A bar for the relative formula mass of Ca(NO3)2.4H2O, 236, split into Ca(NO3)2, 164, and four waters of 18, 72</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"><rect x="20" y="56" width="360" height="34" rx="3"/><path d="M270.2 56 L270.2 90"/><path d="M20 104 V112 H270.2 V104"/><path d="M270.2 104 V112 H380 V104"/></g><g font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor"><text x="20" y="30" font-size="14" text-anchor="start" font-weight="600">Ca(NO₃)₂·4H₂O: Mr 236</text><text x="145.1" y="79" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">Ca(NO₃)₂</text><text x="325.1" y="79" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">4H₂O</text><text x="145.1" y="132" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">164</text><text x="325.1" y="132" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">4 × 18 = 72</text></g></svg>
caption: A hydrate's Mr is the salt's Mr plus the water's.

md: The water is part of the solid, so a hydrate's Mr is the salt's Mr plus the water's. Each $\ce{H2O}$ is $2 \times 1 + 16 = 18$, so n waters add $n \times 18$. Work out the salt first, counting every atom: a number after a bracket multiplies everything inside it.

title: Why the water counts in the Mr
md: Every unit of the crystal carries its waters with it, so one mole of the hydrate weighs one mole of the salt plus n moles of water.

stem: Calculate the Mr of hydrated calcium nitrate, $\ce{Ca(NO3)2.4H2O}$. (Ca = 40, N = 14, O = 16, H = 1) **[2]**

steps.decision: The salt first, every atom counted: the 2 after the bracket doubles the whole nitrate group.
Four waters, each with a relative mass of 18.
Add the two. Leaving the water out gives the anhydrous salt's Mr, which belongs to a different substance.

prompt: Using Mg = 24, S = 32, O = 16 and H = 1, work out the Mr of MgSO₄·7H₂O.
explain: Follow the three steps of See it: the salt first, MgSO₄ = 24 + 32 + 4 × 16 = 120; then the water, 7 × 18 = 126; then add them: 246.

twin.prompt: Using Zn = 65, N = 14, O = 16 and H = 1, work out the Mr of Zn(NO₃)₂·6H₂O.

alt: A bar for MnSO4.xH2O with Mr 223, split into MnSO4, 151, and x waters making 72.
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 150" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="hy3mnMr"><title id="hy3mnMr">A bar for MnSO4.xH2O with Mr 223, split into MnSO4, 151, and x waters making 72</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"><rect x="20" y="56" width="360" height="34" rx="3"/><path d="M263.8 56 L263.8 90"/><path d="M20 104 V112 H263.8 V104"/><path d="M263.8 104 V112 H380 V104"/></g><g font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor"><text x="20" y="30" font-size="14" text-anchor="start" font-weight="600">MnSO₄·xH₂O: Mr 223</text><text x="141.9" y="79" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">MnSO₄</text><text x="321.9" y="79" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">x waters</text><text x="141.9" y="132" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">151</text><text x="321.9" y="132" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">223 − 151 = 72</text></g></svg>
caption: Take the salt away; what is left of the Mr is water.

md: When the formula has an unknown x and the Mr is given, work backwards: take the salt's Mr away from the hydrate's, and what is left is all water. Each water is 18, so divide by 18 to count the molecules.

stem: Hydrated manganese(II) sulfate, $\ce{MnSO4.xH2O}$, has Mr 223. Find x. (Mn = 55, S = 32, O = 16) **[3]**

steps.decision: The anhydrous salt's Mr comes first.
Everything that is not salt is water of crystallisation.
Stopping at the water's share of the Mr gives a mass, not the number of waters.

prompt: Hydrated iron(III) chloride, FeCl₃·xH₂O, has Mr 270.5. Using Fe = 56 and Cl = 35.5, find x.
explain: Follow the three steps of See it: FeCl₃ = 56 + 3 × 35.5 = 162.5; the water is 270.5 − 162.5 = 108; and 108 ÷ 18 = 6. Stopping at 108 gives the water's mass, not x.

twin.prompt: Potash alum, KAl(SO₄)₂·xH₂O, has Mr 474. Using K = 39, Al = 27, S = 32 and O = 16, find x.

caption: Prescribed practical C5: heat, cool, weigh, and repeat.

md: Heat the hydrated salt in a crucible or an evaporating basin, let it cool, and weigh it. Then **heat, cool and weigh again**, and keep repeating until **two weighings agree**: that is **constant mass**, and nothing more can be driven off. Removing water by heating is a **thermal decomposition**.

stem: A student heats 3.25 g of blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate in an evaporating basin, to constant mass. Describe the method and read the results. **[3]**

steps.working: Weigh the empty basin, 32.15 g, then the basin with the blue crystals, 35.40 g.
steps.decision: Two weighings before any heating: the crystals' mass is the difference.

steps.working: Heat, cool and weigh, four times: 34.71 g, 34.30 g, 34.23 g, 34.23 g.
steps.decision: Let the basin cool before each weighing: a hot basin heats the air above the pan and upsets the reading.

steps.working: The last two readings agree at 34.23 g: constant mass. The solid is now a white powder.
steps.decision: Two equal readings show nothing more is leaving; one reading on its own proves nothing.

prompt: Why is the crucible heated, cooled and weighed again and again until two masses are the same?
options: to make sure all the water of crystallisation has been removed
to let the crucible cool down
to check that the balance is working
answer: to make sure all the water of crystallisation has been removed
explain: While water is still leaving, each heating lowers the mass, as the readings in See it fell from 34.71 g to 34.30 g. Once two readings agree, nothing more can be driven off, so all the water of crystallisation has been removed.

optionNotes.option: to let the crucible cool down
optionNotes.why: Cooling comes before each weighing, but it is not why the heating is repeated: the repeats are for the water still leaving.

optionNotes.option: to check that the balance is working
optionNotes.why: The readings change because water is leaving the salt, not because the balance is faulty.

twin.prompt: A student's last two weighings are 26.84 g and 26.79 g. What should the student do next?
options: heat, cool and weigh again
record 26.79 g as the constant mass
add more of the hydrated salt
twin.explain: The mass is still falling, so water is still leaving: heat, cool and weigh again until two readings agree.

optionNotes.option: record 26.79 g as the constant mass
optionNotes.why: The two readings differ, so the mass has not stopped changing yet; constant mass needs two that agree.

optionNotes.option: add more of the hydrated salt
optionNotes.why: Adding salt changes the sample; the water already in it has not all gone yet.

md: A results table asks for three masses, each a subtraction: take the container's mass from the first reading and from the constant mass, then take one from the other for the water. Keep two decimal places, as the balance gives them.

stem: The basin weighed 32.15 g. Use the readings above to find the mass of hydrated salt, of anhydrous salt and of water lost. **[3]**

steps.decision: Take the basin's mass away first.
Use the constant mass, the last reading, never the first heating.
Hydrated minus anhydrous, to two decimal places.

prompt: A crucible weighs 21.30 g, with hydrated sodium carbonate 24.16 g, and 22.36 g at constant mass. What mass of water was lost, in g?
explain: Take both masses from the crucible's, as steps 1 and 2 of See it did: the hydrated salt is 24.16 − 21.30 = 2.86 g and the anhydrous salt 22.36 − 21.30 = 1.06 g, so the water is 2.86 − 1.06 = 1.80 g.

twin.prompt: An evaporating basin weighs 30.08 g, 32.53 g with a hydrated salt, and 31.67 g at constant mass. What is the mass of the anhydrous salt, in g?
twin.explain: The anhydrous salt is what stays at constant mass: 31.67 − 30.08 = 1.59 g.

alt: One CuSO4 unit beside five water molecules: 0.013 mol of CuSO4 and 0.065 mol of water, a ratio of 1 to 5.
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 176" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="hy3cumol"><title id="hy3cumol">One copper(II) sulfate unit beside five water molecules: 0.013 mol of CuSO4 and 0.065 mol of water, a ratio of 1 to 5</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"><rect x="30" y="66" width="34" height="34" rx="3"/><circle cx="130" cy="72" r="12"/><circle cx="172" cy="72" r="12"/><circle cx="214" cy="72" r="12"/><circle cx="256" cy="72" r="12"/><circle cx="298" cy="72" r="12"/></g><g font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor"><text x="47" y="52" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="600">CuSO₄</text><text x="214" y="44" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="600">H₂O</text><text x="47" y="128" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">0.013 mol</text><text x="214" y="150" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">0.065 mol</text></g></svg>
caption: x is a ratio of particles, so it comes from moles.

md: The formula counts particles, so x is a ratio of **moles**: the moles of water lost divided by the moles of anhydrous salt. Find each with moles = mass ÷ Mr, using 18 for water and the anhydrous salt's own Mr.

title: Divide the moles
md: Summer 2023's C2 Higher report: most candidates found the moles of water and of the anhydrous salt, but very few went on to use them to reach x.

stem: The copper(II) sulfate above lost 1.17 g of water and left 2.08 g of anhydrous $\ce{CuSO4}$ (Mr 160). Find x in $\ce{CuSO4.xH2O}$. **[3]**

steps.decision: Moles = mass ÷ Mr, and water's Mr is 18.
The anhydrous salt's mass over its own Mr, not the hydrate's.
Water's moles on top: x waters for every one salt unit.

prompt: 4.88 g of hydrated barium chloride, BaCl₂·xH₂O, leaves 4.16 g at constant mass. Using Mr(BaCl₂) = 208 and Mr(H₂O) = 18, find x.
explain: Follow the three steps of See it: the water is 4.88 − 4.16 = 0.72 g, which is 0.72 ÷ 18 = 0.04 mol; the salt is 4.16 ÷ 208 = 0.02 mol; and 0.04 ÷ 0.02 = 2.

twin.prompt: 9.55 g of hydrated borax, Na₂B₄O₇·xH₂O, leaves 5.05 g at constant mass. Using Mr(Na₂B₄O₇) = 202 and Mr(H₂O) = 18, find x.

text: 7. Why x uses moles, not masses

alt: Two bars for the masses, 2.08 g of CuSO4 and 1.17 g of water, above one salt unit beside five water molecules.
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 210" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="hy3why"><title id="hy3why">Two bars for the masses, 2.08 g of CuSO4 and 1.17 g of water, above one salt unit beside five water molecules</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"><rect x="120" y="22" width="230" height="22" rx="3"/><rect x="120" y="58" width="129.4" height="22" rx="3"/><rect x="30" y="128" width="30" height="30" rx="3"/><circle cx="120" cy="143" r="11"/><circle cx="160" cy="143" r="11"/><circle cx="200" cy="143" r="11"/><circle cx="240" cy="143" r="11"/><circle cx="280" cy="143" r="11"/></g><g font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor"><text x="110" y="38" font-size="14" text-anchor="end">CuSO₄</text><text x="110" y="74" font-size="14" text-anchor="end">water</text><text x="358" y="38" font-size="14" text-anchor="start">2.08 g</text><text x="257.4" y="74" font-size="14" text-anchor="start">1.17 g</text><text x="45" y="116" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">1 unit</text><text x="200" y="116" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">5 molecules</text><text x="200" y="196" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">moles: 0.013 to 0.065, so 1 : 5</text></g></svg>
caption: More salt than water by mass; five waters to each salt unit by particles.

md: Equal masses are not equal numbers of particles. A water molecule has a relative mass of 18; a unit of $\ce{CuSO4}$ has 160, almost 9 times as much. So a sample can hold more salt than water by mass and still hold five waters for every salt unit: only moles count particles.

stem: Compare the copper(II) sulfate's masses with its moles.

steps.working: Masses: 2.08 g of salt against 1.17 g of water: more salt.
steps.decision: By mass, the salt is the larger share.

steps.working: Moles: 0.013 of salt against 0.065 of water, which is 1 : 5.
steps.decision: By particles, the water outnumbers the salt five to one.

steps.working: Only the mole ratio gives the formula: $\ce{CuSO4.5H2O}$.
steps.decision: The formula counts particles, which masses alone cannot do.

prompt: A student divides the mass of water lost by the mass of anhydrous salt to find x. Why does this not work?
options: x is a ratio of particles, and equal masses are not equal numbers of particles
the two masses should be added, not divided
the mass of water should be divided by 16 first
answer: x is a ratio of particles, and equal masses are not equal numbers of particles
explain: Look at the comparison in See it: by mass there was more salt than water, yet by particles there were five waters to each salt unit, because a salt unit is far heavier than a water molecule. x counts particles, so it needs moles.

optionNotes.option: the two masses should be added, not divided
optionNotes.why: Adding them gives the hydrate's mass, not a ratio; x compares numbers of particles, which needs moles.

optionNotes.option: the mass of water should be divided by 16 first
optionNotes.why: Water's Mr is 18, not 16, and the salt's mass must become moles too: each mass is divided by its own Mr.

twin.prompt: In a sample, the masses of water and of anhydrous salt are almost equal. What does that tell you about x?
options: nothing on its own: the masses must first be turned into moles
x is 1
x is about 2
twin.answer: nothing on its own: the masses must first be turned into moles
twin.explain: Equal masses hold different numbers of particles when the salt unit and the water molecule have different masses. Turn both into moles first; only their ratio gives x.

optionNotes.why: Equal masses would mean equal particles only if a salt unit weighed the same as a water molecule, which it does not.
No ratio can be read from masses alone; each mass must be divided by its own Mr first.

alt: Two copper atoms beside one oxygen atom in a dashed box, worked from 0.06 mol of copper and 0.03 mol of oxygen: the simplest whole-number ratio, 2 to 1.

caption: Moles of each element, then the simplest whole-number ratio.

md: An **empirical formula** is the simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms of each element in a compound; a **molecular formula** gives the actual number of each atom in one molecule. From masses: divide each element's mass by its Ar, then divide by the smallest.

stem: 3.84 g of copper combines with 0.48 g of oxygen. Find the empirical formula of the oxide. (Cu = 64, O = 16) **[3]**

steps.decision: Each element's mass over its own Ar.
The smallest becomes 1, so the others show the whole-number ratio.
Write the ratio as the formula, the metal first.

title: GCSE Chemistry Revision "Empirical Formula"
why: The same method on other compounds; made for another exam board, and the method is the same for CCEA.

prompt: 4.48 g of copper forms 5.60 g of copper oxide. Using Cu = 64 and O = 16, give the empirical formula of the oxide.
explain: The oxygen is 5.60 − 4.48 = 1.12 g. Moles, as in step 1 of See it: Cu 4.48 ÷ 64 = 0.07 and O 1.12 ÷ 16 = 0.07. Divided by the smaller that is 1 : 1, so CuO.

twin.prompt: 1.20 g of magnesium forms 2.00 g of magnesium oxide. Using Mg = 24 and O = 16, give the empirical formula of the oxide.

text: 9. From percentages to a molecular formula (Higher)

md: Percentages work the same way: in 100 g of the compound, each percentage is a mass in grams. A molecule is a whole number of empirical units, so divide the molecule's Mr by the empirical formula's Mr and multiply the formula by the answer.

stem: A hydrocarbon contains 80.0% carbon and 20.0% hydrogen by mass, and its Mr is 30. Find its empirical and molecular formulae. (C = 12, H = 1) **[3]**

steps.decision: Each percentage is a mass in 100 g; divide it by its Ar.
Divide by the smaller to reach whole numbers.
The molecular formula is the empirical one multiplied by that whole number.

prompt: A compound has the empirical formula CH₂ and a relative formula mass of 42. Give its molecular formula.
explain: CH₂ has Mr 14, and 42 ÷ 14 = 3, as step 3 of See it divided 30 by 15, so the molecule is 3 CH₂ units: C₃H₆.

twin.prompt: A compound has the empirical formula CH and a relative formula mass of 26. Give its molecular formula.
twin.explain: CH has Mr 13, and 26 ÷ 13 = 2, so the molecule is 2 CH units: C₂H₂.

alt: An evaporating basin sitting on a gauze on a three-legged tripod, heated by a Bunsen burner on a mat, drawn as a flat two-dimensional section with each part labelled.

md: **Define it exactly** (2023, 2024, 2025). Water of crystallisation is water **chemically bonded into the crystal structure**: two ideas, and the 2024 scheme gave each a mark. Hydrated means it contains water of crystallisation.
**Colours, both ways** (Unit 7, 2023 and 2025). Heating turns blue copper(II) sulfate crystals into a white powder; adding water to the white powder turns it blue again, which is the test for water.
**The dehydration equation** (2024). The hydrate gives the anhydrous salt and all its water, the number kept: $\ce{CaCl2.6H2O -> CaCl2 + 6H2O}$.
**Draw the apparatus** (2025). The report found many diagrams 3-D, tripods drawn with four legs and labels missing: draw a flat section, assembled and labelled.

stem: Draw and label the apparatus, assembled, for heating a hydrated salt in an evaporating basin. **[4]**

steps.working: Draw the tripod as a flat section: two of its three legs show.
steps.decision: A flat section is what the scheme recognises; a 3-D or four-legged tripod lost the mark.

steps.working: Put the gauze across the top of the tripod, and the evaporating basin on the gauze.
steps.decision: Assembled, each piece where it sits, not drawn apart.

steps.working: Draw the Bunsen burner underneath, and label all four parts.
steps.decision: A part without its label earns nothing.

prompt: A question asks you to draw and label the apparatus, set up, for heating a hydrated salt. Which drawing earns the marks?
options: a flat section, assembled, with each piece labelled
a 3-D sketch of each piece
the pieces drawn apart, with arrows between them
answer: a flat section, assembled, with each piece labelled
explain: The marks go to recognisable pieces, put together as they would be used, and labelled, as See it built the drawing step by step. A 3-D sketch is hard to read, and pieces drawn apart are not set up.

optionNotes.why: It looks more real, but the 2025 report found 3-D diagrams losing marks: the scheme wants a flat, labelled section.

optionNotes.option: the pieces drawn apart, with arrows between them
optionNotes.why: Drawn apart, the apparatus is not set up; the scheme wants the gauze on the tripod and the basin on the gauze.

twin.prompt: A crucible is heated on a tripod instead of an evaporating basin. What does the crucible rest in?
options: a pipeclay triangle
a gauze
a heatproof mat
twin.explain: A crucible sits in a pipeclay triangle across the tripod, as in the crucible drawing of section 4; a gauze holds a basin, and the mat goes under the burner.

optionNotes.why: A gauze carries a flat-bottomed basin; a small crucible is held in a pipeclay triangle so the flame can reach it.
The mat protects the bench under the Bunsen burner; it does not hold the crucible.

text: 11. Going further: x from a percentage

alt: A bar for the whole mass of gypsum, CaSO4.xH2O, split into 79.1% that remains as anhydrous calcium sulfate and 20.9% driven off as water.

caption: Only a percentage is given: it is the salt's share of the hydrate's Mr.

md: The hardest shape gives only the percentage of the mass left after heating. That percentage is the anhydrous salt's share of the hydrate's Mr, so the Mr follows, and then x.

title: Where the specification stops
md: Naming hydrates with prefixes such as pentahydrate is not required by the CCEA Double Award specification.

stem: Gypsum is hydrated calcium sulfate, $\ce{CaSO4.xH2O}$. It keeps 79.1% of its mass when heated to constant mass. Find x. (Ca = 40, S = 32, O = 16) **[3]**

steps.decision: What remains is the salt, so its Mr is 79.1% of the hydrate's.
Dividing by the decimal of the percentage scales the salt's share up to the whole. The percentage was rounded, so round the Mr to a whole number.
The rest of the Mr is water: divide by 18 to count the molecules.

prompt: Hydrated sodium ethanoate, CH₃COONa·xH₂O, keeps 60.3% of its mass when heated to constant mass. Using Mr(CH₃COONa) = 82, find x.
explain: Follow See it: the hydrate's Mr is 82 ÷ 0.603 = 136, the water is 136 − 82 = 54, and 54 ÷ 18 = 3.

twin.prompt: Hydrated lithium sulfate, Li₂SO₄·xH₂O, keeps 85.9% of its mass when heated to constant mass. Using Mr(Li₂SO₄) = 110, find x.
twin.explain: The hydrate's Mr is 110 ÷ 0.859 = 128; the water is 128 − 110 = 18, and 18 ÷ 18 = 1: one water for each unit, written Li₂SO₄·H₂O.

md:
Define water of crystallisation, hydrated and anhydrous; a hydrate's Mr is the salt's + n × 18.
Find x from the Mr: take the salt away and divide the rest by 18.
Heat to constant mass, then find the masses of salt and water.
Find x from masses or a percentage: moles of water ÷ moles of salt.
Find empirical formulae from masses or percentages, and molecular formulae from the Mr.

Hydrated salts are Question 5 of recent C2 papers on both tiers and practical C5 in Unit 7. Foundation asks for the terms, an Mr, the method and the masses; Higher adds x and empirical formulae, where the scheme wants the working shown. Stuck? Write the three masses first: hydrated, anhydrous and water.
